Pregnancy

Passionflower in pregnancy: why medicinal use is discouraged

Updated: October 12, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Passionflower is promoted for calm and sleep, but medicinal use is not recommended during pregnancy. It may stimulate uterine contractions, and adequate pregnancy-safety data are lacking. This does not mean that every accidental exposure causes miscarriage or early birth. If you have used it, seek advice with the exact product rather than assuming either that harm is certain or that “natural” means safe.

Which passionflower is meant?

The medicinal plant is Passiflora incarnata, a climbing vine with lobed leaves and white-and-purple flowers. Other passionflower species, ornamental plants and products sold under similar names are not automatically equivalent. A description or photograph cannot safely identify a plant for collection or use.

Herbal preparations commonly use dried above-ground parts in teas, powders or extracts. Different plant parts, concentrations and additional ingredients matter. A passionflower medicine is not interchangeable with edible passionfruit or a small food flavouring. General statements about food use do not establish a safe medicinal dose for pregnancy.

What evidence supports its uses?

Limited research in nonpregnant adults suggests possible effects on anxiety or total sleep time, but conclusions are uncertain and results for falling or staying asleep are mixed. EMA traditional-use recognition for mild mental stress and sleep is based on long-standing use, not firm proof from high-quality trials. It does not override pregnancy precautions.

There is no established special pregnancy benefit. Flavonoids, alkaloids or antioxidant activity do not by themselves prove a treatment. A plant containing active compounds can still have uncertain clinical effects, variable strength and risks. Do not use a general adult trial or a “natural calming” label as pregnancy-safety evidence.

Do not treat broad traditional claims as prescriptions

Claims include pain and inflammation relief, immune support, prevention of breast, liver, stomach or prostate cancer, prevention of Alzheimer’s disease, depression or ADHD treatment, and help with opioid withdrawal or muscle spasms. These are not established pregnancy treatments. In particular, opioid dependence or withdrawal needs specialist care, not a home herbal plan.

Claims also cover asthma, ulcers, diarrhoea, indigestion, irregular heartbeat, blood-vessel widening, atherosclerosis, blood pressure, cholesterol, type 2 diabetes, menstrual pain, premenstrual symptoms and menopause. Neither laboratory findings nor traditional use justify substituting passionflower for assessment or prescribed treatment. Persistent symptoms require care directed at their cause.

Why avoid it during pregnancy?

NCCIH advises against passionflower during pregnancy because it may induce uterine contractions. The EMA monograph also advises against use because pregnancy and breastfeeding safety are unestablished. A precaution based on possible contractions and missing data is different from a measured probability of miscarriage after a particular dose.

No safe pregnancy dose, trimester, treatment duration or medicinal-tea strength has been established. Do not use it to bring on labour or end a pregnancy. Ordinary food-flavouring statements and short-term adult tea studies do not make a concentrated preparation or a medicinal drink acceptable during pregnancy.

Side effects and uncertainty about serious harm

Drowsiness, dizziness, confusion and impaired coordination can occur. If affected, do not drive or operate machinery. Nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, rapid heartbeat or low blood pressure may be reported or have other causes; do not assume they are harmless or that they prove passionflower toxicity.

Serious rhythm and other adverse reports often lack enough information to establish causation. LiverTox has not convincingly linked passionflower alone to clinical liver injury, while noting limited safety studies. That is not proof of pregnancy safety. Neither an unverified list of inevitable liver damage nor an assurance of no possible harm accurately reflects the evidence.

Medicines, anaesthesia and product quality

Passionflower can add to the effects of sedating medicines or anaesthetic drugs. Tell your pharmacist and maternity or surgical team about it, particularly if a procedure is planned or you used it within the previous two weeks. Do not delay an urgent procedure or choose a stopping interval yourself; the team needs the information to plan safe care.

Review all ingredients and prescriptions, including sleep, mental-health, diabetes and blood-pressure medicines. Not every member of these medicine groups has a proven interaction with passionflower. Mixtures, alcohol-containing tinctures and undeclared ingredients add uncertainty. Do not stop an essential prescription or replace it with a herb without your prescriber’s advice.

If you have already taken a tea or supplement

Avoid further non-essential medicinal passionflower and contact a pharmacist, midwife or clinician for individual advice. Keep the packaging and note the species if stated, all ingredients, amount, concentration, time, pregnancy stage and symptoms. A mixed sleep product needs review of the whole formula, not just the word passionflower.

One exposure is not a diagnosis of harm, and a symptom-free interval does not establish safety. Ask whether any assessment or follow-up is needed; there is no universal extra-scan schedule or reliable home test for this exposure. Do not try to induce vomiting, take another herb to counter it or use a herbal recipe for contractions.

Get support for sleep, anxiety or low mood

Tell your maternity team if worry, poor sleep or low mood is affecting daily life. They can assess causes and discuss practical sleep support, talking therapies such as CBT and, when appropriate, medicines chosen for your situation. Pregnancy does not mean that every effective treatment must be stopped.

Regular routines, appropriate activity and support from trusted people may help, but they do not replace care for persistent symptoms. If already treated for a mental-health condition, contact your prescriber rather than stopping abruptly. If you cannot keep yourself safe, seek immediate emergency help; a calming supplement is not a crisis treatment.

Symptoms should guide how urgently you get help

Contact maternity care immediately for any vaginal bleeding, leaking fluid, less fetal movement than usual or possible labour before 37 weeks. Do not wait until tomorrow. New pelvic pain during possible pregnancy also needs urgent assessment even without a positive pregnancy test. These symptoms do not prove that a herb caused a problem.

Get emergency help now for severe or worsening abdominal or pelvic pain, pain with movement or touch, or pelvic pain with faintness, dizziness, shoulder-tip pain, heavy bleeding, breathing difficulty or sudden confusion. Bleeding with severe pain, shoulder pain, feeling sick, faintness, dizziness or loss of consciousness is also an emergency. Sudden lip or tongue swelling, breathing difficulty, a new seizure or loss of consciousness requires emergency help. Do not drive yourself or wait for a supplement to wear off.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Avoid starting medicinal passionflower during pregnancy. Ask a pharmacist or maternity clinician about the actual ingredients rather than relying on adult sleep studies or a natural label.

For sleep, anxiety or mood concerns, seek an individual treatment plan and keep essential prescribed treatment until you have discussed changes. Tell the team about supplements before anaesthesia or procedures.

After an exposure, record the product, amount and timing and seek advice without assuming certain harm. Contact maternity care promptly for warning signs and use emergency care for severe pain, bleeding with serious symptoms or breathing/consciousness changes.

How BeMama can help

Use BeMama to note the exact passionflower product and ingredients, amount and time taken, pregnancy stage, sleep or mood symptoms, other medicines and questions for your appointment. It cannot identify a herb, establish fetal safety, predict individual harm or decide how urgently symptoms need care. Uncertain benefit and a reason to avoid medicinal use do not mean one exposure inevitably harmed a pregnancy; a natural label does not prove safety either. Accurate notes can support a clinical discussion, but must not delay medical or maternity care.

When to seek help

Avoid medicinal passionflower in pregnancy and do not use it to induce labour or end pregnancy. Report use and ingredients; do not stop essential medicines or try to counter an exposure yourself. Call maternity care immediately for bleeding, leaking fluid, reduced fetal movement or possible labour before 37 weeks. Severe/worsening abdominal or pelvic pain, pain on movement/touch, or pelvic pain with faintness, dizziness, shoulder-tip pain, heavy bleeding, breathing difficulty or sudden confusion requires emergency care. Bleeding with severe pain, shoulder pain, feeling sick, faintness, dizziness or loss of consciousness also needs emergency help. Sudden lip/tongue swelling, a new seizure or loss of consciousness are emergencies. Do not drive yourself or wait for the herb to clear.

Evidence notes updated: October 12, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Medicinal passionflower is discouraged in pregnancy because of possible contractions and insufficient safety data.
  • Adult sleep or anxiety research does not establish a pregnancy benefit or dose.
  • Food, medicinal tea and concentrated extracts are different exposures.
  • Report the exact product, ingredients and timing after use; do not assume certain harm.
  • Seek timely maternity care for bleeding, fluid, movement or labour changes and emergency care for serious symptoms.

Frequently asked questions

What is passionflower, and do its plant compounds prove benefits?

The medicinal plant is Passiflora incarnata, commonly used as above-ground parts in herbal preparations. Active compounds or antioxidant activity do not establish effective treatment or pregnancy safety. Similar plant names are not enough to identify a safe product.

Are its traditional uses proven treatments?

No. Broad claims about cancer, heart or metabolic disease, digestion, hormones, ADHD or opioid withdrawal are not established pregnancy treatments. Mild stress and sleep traditional-use recognition is not proof for every claim or permission to use it while pregnant.

What side effects can occur?

Drowsiness, dizziness, confusion and impaired coordination are possible. Digestive or cardiac symptoms deserve assessment rather than an assumption about cause. Serious case reports do not reliably establish rates or causation, and passionflower alone is not convincingly linked to clinical liver injury in LiverTox.

Is medicinal passionflower safe during pregnancy?

It is not recommended. Possible uterine contractions and insufficient safety data support avoiding it. No safe dose or trimester is established, but this does not prove that every accidental exposure causes miscarriage or early birth.

Is a weak tea or food flavouring an exception?

A general statement about small food-flavouring use is not a safe medicinal-tea rule for pregnancy. Strength, plant part and ingredients vary. Do not treat adult short-term use information as permission to start a pregnancy remedy.

What if I took it before knowing I was pregnant?

Avoid further non-essential use and ask for individual advice with packaging, amount, timing and pregnancy stage. Do not assume harm is certain, induce vomiting or try a counteracting herb. The clinician can decide whether assessment is needed.

Should I stop my prescribed medicine instead?

No. Speak with your prescriber before changing essential treatment. Report supplements and any planned anaesthetic procedure; passionflower may add to sedation, while not every claimed medicine interaction is established.

When do I need immediate help?

Contact maternity care immediately for bleeding, fluid leakage, reduced movement or suspected labour before 37 weeks. Severe or worsening pelvic/abdominal pain, pain on movement/touch or pelvic pain with faintness, dizziness, shoulder-tip pain, heavy bleeding or breathing difficulty needs emergency care. Bleeding with severe pain, shoulder pain, feeling sick, faintness, dizziness or loss of consciousness is also an emergency. Seek emergency help for sudden airway swelling, a new seizure or loss of consciousness; do not drive or wait for the herb to clear.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
